newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz to pursue secularist govt search.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz to pursue secularist govt search.

text.p: Turkish conservative leader Mesut Yilmaz said he had received the backing of the president to pursue his search to form a secularist alliance despite efforts by the ruling Islamists to de-rail his plan.
"The president asked me to continue in my duty," Yilmaz told reporters after meeting with President Suleyman Demirel after a day of further negotiations to put together a viable coalition.

Earlier on Wednesday caretaker Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan hit back at Yilmaz's bid to forge an opposition alliance, presenting a petition signed by a majority of MPs rejecting a plan to keep his Islamists from power.

The announcement highlighted the difficulty faced by Yilmaz in uniting the country's splintered secularist parties against Erbakan, who was edged out of power last week under pressure from the secularist establishment.

"A total of 278 deputies have signed up to reject a Yilmaz government," Erbakan told a news conference. He produced what he said was a petition of signatures from MPs against plans for a coalition under secularist Yilmaz.
Yilmaz, appointed by the president last week to form a government, is just short of the majority needed to win a confidence vote in the 550-seat parliament.
He has won the backing of secularist MPs from the left and right but will rely on support from dissidents in the rival conservative True Path Party, whose leader Tansu Ciller is allied with Erbakan.
The resignation of a deputy from the True Path Party on Wednesday gave a small boost to Yilmaz's campaign.

"I am resigning from the party today to avoid going through a disciplinary process similar to the inquisition courts," MP Hasan Denizkurdu said in a four-page resignation letter to the speaker's office.
Denizkurdu was facing party disciplinary action for refusing to oppose Yilmaz's bid to form a secularist government in place of the Islamist-led coalition.
Despite the resignation, True Path officials said Ciller had gained assurances from all but two of her MPs that they would not vote for the proposed secularist coalition.
Ciller, the pro-Western foreign minister, heads an opposing alliance with the Islamists that is vying for power to take the country to early elections.
She dropped strong criticism of the Islamists last year and joined them in office after Yilmaz backed corruption charges against her when they were in a conservative coalition together.
At a news conference, Yilmaz said he was confident he would be able to win clear parliamentary support and cast doubt on True Path unity against him.

"The government that I will form will win a confidence vote and it will not be a matter of winning by a hair's breadth," he told reporters. "We will see about those who signed the petition in the days ahead."
He has given himself until early next week to present Demirel a government list to replace Erbakan's one-year-old government.
Erbakan resigned to resolve a growing dispute with the military over the rising profile of Islam in public life.

The military-dominated National Security Council, which launched an anti-Islamist campaign in February, said on Wednesday it had reviewed government efforts to crack down on rising religious activism.

A bitter feud between Motherland Party leader Yilmaz and rival conservative leader Ciller is the main obstacle in the way of a secularist alliance. The two met on Tuesday for 20 minutes of talks where Ciller rejected an offer to support Yilmaz.

He said he would not meet Ciller again in the search for a coalition unless she recognises him as prime minister-designate. "It is impossible for me to meet Mrs Ciller if she does not change her attitude," Yilmaz said.
The Turkish stock market, buffeted in the last two days by speculation over the prospects for such a coalition, drifted 0.65 percent lower on Wednesday in quiet trading.
